subject: Liu et al. (1997)
object: Liu et al. (1997) inactivated the Col3a1 gene in mouse embryonic stem cells by homologous recombination and derived homozygous mutant mice from heterozygous intercrosses. About 10% of homozygous mutant mice survived to adulthood but had a much shorter life span than wildtype mice; the major cause of death was rupture of the major blood vessels, similar to patients with type IV Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Ultrastructural analysis of mutant tissues showed that type III collagen is essential for normal collagen I fibrillogenesis in the cardiovascular system and other organs.

subject: Schwarze et al. (2001)
object: Schwarze et al. (2001) identified three heterozygous frameshift mutations in the COL3A1 gene (1832delAA, 413delC, and 555delT) in probands with a phenotype similar to vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. The mutations led to premature termination codons in exons 27, 6, and 9, respectively. The mRNA from each mutant allele was transcribed efficiently but rapidly degraded, presumably by nonsense-mediated decay, which made the allele product unstable.

subject: Schwarze et al. (2001)
object: In a fourth patient with a phenotype similar to vascular EDS, Schwarze et al. (2001) identified a point mutation in the final exon of the COL3A1 gene, 4294C-T, that produced a premature termination codon (Arg1432Ter). The mutant mRNA was stable, but it led to synthesis of a truncated protein that was not incorporated into mature type III procollagen molecules.

subject: Schwarze et al. (2001)
object: Schwarze et al. (2001) reported that in all 4 probands with COL3A1 haploinsufficiency mutations, the presenting feature was vascular aneurysm or rupture. The resulting phenotype overlapped with that of vascular EDS.

subject: Schwarze et al. (2001)
object: Schwarze et al. (2001) concluded that null mutations in COL3A1 produce phenotypes that overlap with vascular EDS. In COL1A1 and COL2A1, by contrast, null mutations produce milder phenotypes than mutations that alter protein sequence. The authors suggested that the major effect of many dominant mutations in the 'minor' collagen genes may be expressed through protein deficiency rather than through incorporation of structurally altered molecules into fibrils. They noted that mice heterozygous for Col3a1 null alleles have no identified phenotype.

subject: Plancke et al. (2009)
object: Plancke et al. (2009) studied a young girl with recessive Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. She was born to consanguineous, healthy parents and met the criteria for laboratory testing for vascular EDS.

subject: Plancke et al. (2009)
object: Plancke et al. (2009) sequenced the entire COL3A1 cDNA of the proband and found a homozygous 1-bp duplication (c.479dupT) that causes a frameshift and a premature termination codon (p.Lys161GlnfsX45). Testing of genomic DNA showed that she inherited the variant from each of her parents.

subject: Plancke et al. (2009)
object: In the proband, Plancke et al. (2009) used RT-PCR, quantitative PCR, immunohistochemistry and Western blot to study expression. They found strong mRNA decay and no type III collagen.

subject: Plancke et al. (2009)
object: Plancke et al. (2009) reported that the proband's heterozygous parents and other healthy relatives in earlier generations, who were expected to have COL3A1 haploinsufficiency, did not show features of vascular EDS. The authors suggested that COL3A1 haploinsufficiency has a stochastic effect in humans. They proposed this could be explained by how efficient nonsense-mediated mRNA decay is, and by the resulting dominant-negative effect, depending on where the mutation lies and/or on modifying factors.

subject: Jeong et al. (2012)
object: Jeong et al. (2012) found that Col3a1-null mice had a cobblestone-like cortical malformation, with breakdown of the pial basement membrane (BM), neuronal overmigration, detachment of radial glial endfeet, and marginal zone heterotopias. All Col3a1-null mice examined at embryonic day (E) 18.5 had neuronal ectopias on the brain surface. These ectopias contained neurons from both deep and superficial cortical layers (Cux1+, Tbr1+, and CTIP2+), which mirrored Gpr56-null mice. Ectopia penetrance was 23 of 28 in null embryos, 0 of 12 in heterozygotes, and 0 of 20 in wildtype embryos.

subject: Jeong et al. (2012)
object: Jeong et al. (2012) found that in Col3a1-null mice the pial BM formed normally at E10.5, even though collagen III was absent. Regional breakdown of the BM, with neuronal overmigration, appeared in about half of E11.5 embryos and in all embryos older than E12.5. In the mutants, radial glial endfeet protruded through the breached BM, and Cajal-Retzius cells and calbindin-positive interneurons were misplaced into the ectopias.

subject: Jeong et al. (2012)
object: Jeong et al. (2012) found that meningeal fibroblasts from Col3a1-null mice had no obvious defects, and that the level of glycosylated alpha-dystroglycan in mutant brains was unchanged. They suggested that collagen III, the ligand of GPR56, regulates cortical development independently of the dystroglycan pathway, and that the dyslamination results from the absence of collagen III rather than from a defect in meningeal fibroblasts.

subject: Jeong et al. (2012)
object: Jeong et al. (2012) noted that homozygous Col3a1 deletion mostly caused perinatal lethality, with only about 5% of mice surviving to adulthood. The survivors had features resembling vascular-type (type IV) Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, including rupture of large blood vessels. Losing one allele caused no obvious defects. The authors postulated that biallelic COL3A1 mutations in humans may be associated with a lethal form of cobblestone lissencephaly similar to Walker-Warburg syndrome.

subject: Jørgensen et al. (2015)
object: Jørgensen et al. (2015) described a boy (III-2) who was born with right-sided clubfoot and had a unilateral testicular hydrocele, crowded teeth, retrognathia, long slender fingers, and pale translucent skin. He died unexpectedly at age 15 years after a week of backache. Autopsy showed dissections of the thoracic aorta, the right renal artery and the left femoral artery, with extensive bleeding and cystic medial necrosis of the aortic wall. The brain looked macroscopically normal, but neither brain imaging nor histological cerebral examination was performed.

subject: Jørgensen et al. (2015)
object: Jørgensen et al. (2015) described the proband's sister (III-3). She had long slender fingers, small-joint hypermobility, translucent skin with visible veins, the facial features of vascular EDS, spontaneous rupture of small superficial vessels, intermittent abdominal pain with blood in the stool, and migraine with aura. By age 19 to 20 years she had dissections of both internal carotid arteries and a stenosis of the right external iliac artery, while aortic dimensions were normal. Brain MRI showed bilateral thickened frontoparietal cortices with small gyri, consistent with pachy-micropolygyria. Despite this, her cognition was normal, her neurologic examination was normal, she had never had seizures, and her motor and language development had been normal.

subject: Jørgensen et al. (2015)
object: Jørgensen et al. (2015) found that both affected sibs were compound heterozygous for 2 COL3A1 variants. One was a nonsense variant, c.1786C>T (p.Arg596Ter), in exon 26, which encodes part of the triple helical domain. They inherited it from their father, who was clinically unaffected at age 63. The proband had no variants in FBN1, TGFBR1, or TGFBR2. The unaffected brother carried neither COL3A1 variant.

subject: Jørgensen et al. (2015)
object: Jørgensen et al. (2015) found that the second COL3A1 variant in the affected sibs was a missense variant, c.3851G>A (p.Gly1284Glu), in exon 50, which encodes part of the C-terminal propeptide. The sibs inherited it from their mother, who had only partial features of the disorder. The substituted glycine is highly conserved and lies next to a cysteine involved in interchain disulfide bonding, within a calcium-binding region. The authors predicted that the change would slow assembly of the trimer.

subject: Jørgensen et al. (2015)
object: Jørgensen et al. (2015) studied cultured dermal fibroblasts. Cells from the compound heterozygous sister made a reduced amount of type III procollagen, and all of its chains had abnormal electrophoretic mobility, consistent with overmodification. Cells from the mother (missense heterozygote) made mostly normal type III procollagen plus a small amount of slightly overmodified procollagen. Cells from the father (nonsense heterozygote) made a reduced amount of apparently normal type III procollagen.

subject: Jørgensen et al. (2015)
object: Jørgensen et al. (2015) reported marked clinical variation within the family. The father and other paternal relatives who were heterozygous for the nonsense variant had no complications or clinical features of vascular EDS; the paternal grandmother was healthy at 85 years. The mother, heterozygous for the missense variant, had thin skin with visible vessels, reduced elasticity of the ascending aorta, and emphysema, but not the full vascular EDS phenotype by age 60. The authors concluded that biallelic variants give a significantly worse outcome than heterozygous variants.

subject: Jørgensen et al. (2015)
object: Jørgensen et al. (2015) noted that type III collagen is the ligand for GPR56, and that GPR56 variants cause recessive bilateral frontoparietal polymicrogyria. They suggested that the GPR56–type III collagen interaction forms part of a pathway in brain formation, and they proposed a novel syndromic recessive form of vascular EDS that combines tissue fragility with cerebrocortical anomalies. They also acknowledged that the brain findings could be coincidental or caused by variants in a second gene.

subject: Vandervore et al. (2017)
object: Vandervore et al. (2017) reported a family with 2 affected and 2 unaffected sibs in which brain MRI of the affected sibs, as well as of 2 previously reported individuals with bi-allelic COL3A1 mutations, showed a brain phenotype similar to that associated with GPR56 mutations: cobblestone-like cortical malformation, white matter changes, and cerebellar cysts. The authors noted variability of the phenotype across patients.

subject: Vandervore et al. (2017)
object: In 2 sibs with cobblestone-like cortical malformation, white matter changes and cerebellar cysts, Vandervore et al. (2017) identified by exome analysis a novel homozygous variant, c.145C>G (p.Pro49Ala), in exon 2 of the COL3A1 gene. Functional assays were performed on dermal fibroblasts.

subject: Vandervore et al. (2017)
object: Vandervore et al. (2017) concluded that homozygous or compound heterozygous COL3A1 mutations were associated with cobblestone-like malformation in all 3 families reported to date, and suggested that the phenotypic variability indicates that alterations in distinct domains of type III procollagen can lead to different outcomes.

subject: Vandervore et al. (2017)
object: Vandervore et al. (2017) noted that type III procollagen is the ligand of GPR56 (ADGRG1) and that the presence of cobblestone-like malformation in patients with bi-allelic COL3A1 mutations emphasized the critical role of the type III collagen-GPR56 axis and the pial membrane in brain development and cortical lamination.

subject: Horn et al. (2017)
object: Horn et al. (2017) described a 3-year-old girl with developmental delay who was born with bilateral clubfoot, joint laxity, and dysmorphic facial features. At age 2 years she had an aneurysmal brain hemorrhage. Cerebral MRI showed a distinctive pattern of profound cerebral abnormalities, including bilateral frontoparietal polymicrogyria of the cobblestone type.

subject: Horn et al. (2017)
object: In the 3-year-old girl with polymicrogyria and connective tissue features, Horn et al. (2017) identified compound heterozygous COL3A1 variants: a nonsense variant, c.1282C>T (p.Arg428Ter), and a frameshift variant, c.2057delC (p.Pro686LeufsTer105). Both variants were novel.

subject: Horn et al. (2017)
object: Horn et al. (2017) described a second family in which 2 affected sibs had a cobblestone-like cortical malformation, cerebellar cysts, white matter abnormalities, developmental delay, and seizures.

subject: Horn et al. (2017)
object: In 2 sibs with cobblestone-like cortical malformation, cerebellar cysts, and seizures, Horn et al. (2017) identified a homozygous missense variant in COL3A1, reported as c.145C<G (p.Pro49Ala).

subject: Horn et al. (2017)
object: Horn et al. (2017) noted that 3 more families had previously been reported with biallelic COL3A1 variants. All had specific structural brain anomalies, and some had a severe Ehlers-Danlos syndrome phenotype. The brain phenotype was characterized by bilateral frontoparietal cobblestone polymicrogyria, cerebellar microcysts, and white matter abnormalities, and it resembled the neurologic features of patients with autosomal recessive GPR56 mutations.

subject: Horn et al. (2017)
object: Horn et al. (2017) noted that GPR56 acts as a ligand of COL3A1. Consistent with findings in knockout mice, they concluded that collagen III helps regulate cortical development as well as connective tissue formation.
